periods.analysis: We opened the arc with the safety fundamentals where they need to be: Maritime Safety Incidents were 1 count against a target of <=2, and Aviation Safety Incidents were 2 count against a target of <=3. That is green performance in a busy gateway quarter, with Harborview handling summer cruise turns, cargo peaks, and late-bank airport operations without losing operational discipline. The yellow condition is At-Berth Shore Power Utilization at 47.3% against a >=60 target, mainly from missed plug-in windows at Berths 6 and 7 and two vessels arriving without compatible high-voltage connection plans. My read is straightforward: the crews are safe, the system is moving, but our sustainability handoff from berth assignment to vessel connection is not yet tight enough.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green safety results by extending the joint ramp-and-dockside safety walk-throughs on the North Cargo route and Terminal B hardstand from monthly to biweekly through the next peak period. For shore power, assign a 72-hour pre-arrival plug-in confirmation to Port Operations, the shipping agents, and the HarborGrid electrician on duty for every shore-power-capable vessel. The watch item is Berths 6 and 7: track missed connections by cause code each week and escalate any repeat equipment or vessel-readiness failure before the next sailing window.

periods.analysis: Q4 strengthened the safety side: Maritime Safety Incidents improved from 1 count to 0 count, and Aviation Safety Incidents improved from 2 count to 1 count, both green and both the product of disciplined close-call reporting rather than luck. The holiday travel bank and wet-weather container operations were real tests, and the field teams held the line. Shore power moved the wrong way, from 47.3% to 45.7%, a decline of 1.6 percentage points against the >=60 target. The main drag was winter berth switching during Pier East fender work, which left shore-power-ready vessels tied up at non-enabled positions more often than planned.
periods.recommendations: Keep the zero-maritime-incident practice alive by retaining the tug-master pre-job huddle checklist used on Pier East and adding the same checklist to Pier West night moves. Maintain aviation safety gains by continuing the deicing pad radio-readback audit on Taxiway Kilo and Gate 14 alley operations. For shore power, require the berth planner to run a daily “green berth first” assignment check during construction phasing, with any exception signed off by the Seaport duty manager.

periods.analysis: Q1 showed the expected seasonal reset but stayed within safety tolerance: Maritime Safety Incidents rose from 0 count to 1 count, and Aviation Safety Incidents rose from 1 count to 2 count, still green against targets of <=2 and <=3. The incidents were reviewed through the Marine Safety Board and Airport SMS panel, and neither showed a systemic breakdown. Shore power improved from 45.7% to 48.5%, up 2.8 percentage points, which is useful progress but still materially short of the >=60 target. The improvement came after HarborGrid restored the C-Loop cable reel and dispatch began pairing shore-power-capable vessels with Berths 5 through 7 earlier in the rotation.
periods.recommendations: Sustain safety performance by closing every Q1 corrective action in the Intelex log within 30 days, with special attention to the apron service-road crossing near Gate B22 and the container-yard lane at Pier North. Extend the successful C-Loop repair playbook by pre-staging spare cam-lock assemblies and a certified electrician for Friday-to-Monday vessel clusters. The shore-power watch item is schedule integrity: compare planned versus actual green-berth assignments every Monday and remove avoidable late swaps from the rotation.

periods.analysis: Q2 pushed activity hard and the numbers show it: Maritime Safety Incidents increased from 1 count to 2 count, and Aviation Safety Incidents increased from 2 count to 3 count. Both remain green because they are at, not over, the targets of <=2 and <=3, but this is the upper edge of acceptable performance and I do not treat that casually. Shore power inched up from 48.5% to 49.2%, a 0.7 percentage-point gain, still yellow against the >=60 target. The story is a high-throughput quarter where safety controls held, but the plug-in program did not yet scale with cargo, cruise, and international belly-freight demand.
periods.recommendations: Hold a focused Q2 safety stand-down for the two marine incident work groups and the three affected ramp teams, then verify corrective actions during live operations rather than in conference-room signoff. Preserve the green status by adding a second airfield safety officer during the 0600-0900 departure bank and a dock safety lead during double-ship cruise days. For shore power, pilot a “plug-in captain” role on Berths 5, 6, and 7 for 45 days, accountable for cable readiness, vessel coordination, and connection timing from lines-fast to first cargo move.

periods.analysis: Q3 pulled safety back from the Q2 ceiling: Maritime Safety Incidents improved from 2 count to 1 count, and Aviation Safety Incidents improved from 3 count to 2 count, both green. That tells me the stand-downs and added field supervision were not theater; they changed behavior on the ramp and at the berth face. Shore power slipped from 49.2% to 47.6%, down 1.6 percentage points and still yellow against the >=60 target. The slippage tracked to peak cruise calls, one failed transformer temperature sensor on SP-6, and several vessels choosing auxiliary generation during short berth windows.
periods.recommendations: Continue the added field-supervisor model through the next high-volume quarter, but narrow it to the highest-risk windows: first-light aircraft turns and simultaneous container-lash operations. Lock in the safety gains by requiring supervisors to document one corrected unsafe condition per shift, not just attendance at briefings. For shore power, replace the SP-6 temperature sensor, publish minimum plug-in dwell-time rules for short calls, and give cruise agents a pre-arrival go/no-go decision no later than 24 hours before docking.

periods.analysis: Q4 delivered a strong maritime safety result, improving from 1 count to 0 count, while Aviation Safety Incidents held steady at 2 count, still green against the <=3 target. In wet pavement, holiday passenger surge, and shorter daylight, that is the kind of steady execution I expect from a mature airport-seaport organization. Shore power declined again, from 47.6% to 45.8%, down 1.8 percentage points against the >=60 target. This was the second consecutive quarterly decline, and the watch item is no longer just equipment readiness; it is the operating model for assigning, connecting, and enforcing shore-power use during irregular operations.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the zero-maritime-incident quarter by keeping Pier West night-move audits in place and rotating the lessons into the tug contractor scorecard. For aviation, continue the Gate B pushback observer program and add specific monitoring for ground-service-equipment staging during holiday banks. For shore power, convene a 30-day recovery cell with Seaport Operations, HarborGrid, terminal operators, and the top five calling carriers, with a required vessel-by-vessel exception report for every missed eligible connection.

periods.analysis: Q1 stabilized the pattern but did not finish the job: Maritime Safety Incidents moved from 0 count to 1 count, while Aviation Safety Incidents held at 2 count, both green. The single maritime incident was isolated in the incident review, and the aviation number holding flat through storm-diversion days is a credit to airfield operations. Shore power rebounded from 45.8% to 48.7%, up 2.9 percentage points, which is the best quarterly improvement in this sequence but still yellow against the >=60 target. The recovery cell helped by resolving carrier data gaps and restoring predictable connection staffing on the C-Loop, but we still lose too many eligible hours when berth changes occur after pilot boarding.
periods.recommendations: Keep the safety system steady by sustaining the Marine Safety Board weekly review for another quarter and extending airfield FOD sweeps on Taxiways Juliet and Kilo after storm events. Convert the shore-power recovery cell from a meeting into a control tower: one live dashboard, one duty owner, and same-day correction of berth swaps that would strand an eligible vessel away from power. The watch item is late berth reassignment; require Deputy Port Director approval when a shore-power-capable vessel is moved to a non-enabled berth after the 12-hour mark.

periods.analysis: Q2 again reached the top of the green safety band: Maritime Safety Incidents increased from 1 count to 2 count, and Aviation Safety Incidents increased from 2 count to 3 count, both exactly at their targets of <=2 and <=3. I am satisfied they remain green, but being at the ceiling is a warning light, not a victory lap, especially with summer traffic building. Shore power improved from 48.7% to 50.9%, up 2.2 percentage points and the highest result in the eight-quarter arc, yet still yellow versus the >=60 target. The direction is now right, helped by the control-tower dashboard and better carrier compliance, but the gap to 60% remains an operational reliability problem we have to close deliberately.
periods.recommendations: Protect the green safety status by activating the summer surge safety plan: extra ramp marshal coverage for the international arrival bank, dockside spotters during simultaneous cruise and container moves, and weekly executive review of any repeat hazard. Sustain and extend the shore-power gains by making the plug-in captain permanent for enabled berths and tying terminal-operator performance meetings to eligible-hours captured, not just successful connections. Set a Q3 action threshold: if utilization does not continue upward toward the >=60 target by mid-quarter, accelerate the SP-8 commissioning schedule and add carrier-specific compliance notices for vessels that bypass available power.

periods.analysis: Aviation incidents fell to two, but maritime incidents rose to three against a ceiling of two. Shore-power utilization improved to 53.2% yet remains below 60%, while the electrification permit milestone is overdue. An operating improvement does not erase either the safety variance or the longer-term project delay.
periods.recommendations: Assign corrective actions after reviewing the maritime incidents. Confirm a recovery date and outstanding decisions for shore-power permitting, then report operating connections and capital progress separately.
